e current granularity defined in SA5 is per node. From our point of view, for mobility load balance purpose, the granularity of this measurement could be QCI/5QI and ARP level. With this, when performing load balancing, not only the total PRB usage but also the distribution of the PRB usage(i.e.QCI/5QI of the traffic in the cell) could be considered which could achieve better load balancing with QoS of the service considered. Proposal 1: “UL/DL Total PRB Usage” could be collected with “DRB QoS” level. UE throughput • Average UL/DL UE throughput in gNB This measurement provides the average UE throughput in uplink/downlink. This measurement is intended for data bursts that are large enough to require transmissions to be split across multiple slots. The UE data volume refers to the total volume scheduled for each UE regardless if using only primary- or also supplemental aggregated carriers. • Distribution of UL/DL UE throughput in gNB This measurement provides the distribution of the UE throughput in uplink/downlink. This measurement is intended for data bursts that are large enough to require transmissions to be split across multiple slots. The UE data volume refers to the total volume scheduled for each UE regardless if using only primary- or also supplemental aggregated carriers. • Volume of unrestricted UL/DL UE data in gNB This measurement provides the percentage of UL/DL data volume for UEs in the cell that is classified as unrestricted, i.e., when the volume is so low that all data can be transferred in one slot and no UE throughput sample could be calculated. The UE data volume refers to the total volume scheduled for each UE regardless if using only primary- or also supplemental aggregated carriers. Node implements the measurement: In SA5 definition, the UE throughtput is calculated based on RLC layer SDU. If we follow the solution defined in SA5,the measurement should be implemented by DU. RRC connection number • Mean number of RRC Connections This measurement provides the mean number of users in RRC connected mode during each granularity period. • Max number of RRC Connections This measurement provides the maximum number of users in RRC connected mode during each granularity period. Node implements the measurement: Based on SA5 definition, the above measurements should be done by CU. However, in LTE, there are similar measurement i.e Number of active UEs per QCI, if we follow the measurement definition in LTE, the measurement should be done in CU-UP. PDU Session Management • Number of PDU Sessions requested to setup This measurement provides the number of PDU Sessions in the PDU SESSION RESOURCE SETUP REQUESTs received by the gNB from AMF. This measurement is split into subcounters per S-NSSAI. • Number of PDU Sessions successfully setup This measurement provides the number of PDU Sessions successfully setup by the gNB for the PDU SESSION RESOURCE SETUP REQUESTs received from AMF. This measurement is split into subcounters per S-NSSAI. • Number of PDU Sessions failed to setup This measurement provides the number of PDU Sessions failed to setup by the gNB for the PDU SESSION RESOURCE SETUP REQUESTs received from AMF. This measurement is split into subcounters per failure cause. Node implements the measurement: This measurement should be done by CU-CP. Observation: PDU Session Management is neither a L2 measurements nor a L1 measurement. Mobility Management Currently mobility management only includes inter-gNB handovers related statistics. • Number of requested handover preparations This measurement provides the number of handover preparations requested by the source gNB. • Number of successful handover preparations This measurement provides the number of successful handover preparations received by the source NR cell CU. • Number of failed handover preparations This me

n of services at the RAN–CN boundary. Procedure-centric approach – Each legacy procedure may be mapped to a corresponding service, resulting in a model closely aligned with existing procedures defined in NGAP [6], particularly when the procedure is atomic (e.g., Error Indication, NG Reset, etc.). Pros: direct traceability with the existing protocol specification, allowing a relatively straightforward transition from the current procedure-based model, resulting in a lower migration effort. Cons: definition of a large number of narrowly scoped services, potentially resulting in duplicated semantics across services and making it more difficult to introduce richer interaction patterns such as query-based or subscription-based mechanisms. Functional service classes – Services are identified according to higher-level functional capabilities rather than individual procedures. A service may encompass multiple related operations associated with a given functional capability exposed across the RAN–CN boundary. Pros: reduction of service fragmentation, allowing clearer identification of service producers, service consumers, and data ownership following typical service-based interaction models. Cons: Need for mapping identified services to legacy NGAP procedures, as the correspondence is not necessarily one-to-one. The procedure-centric approach can be considered as a transitional option to facilitate migration from legacy NGAP-based interactions, while the functional service class approach may represent a target architecture (e.g., for new services) aligned with service-based principles, consistent with the approach specified in 5G CN [4], where services are defined as functional capabilities decoupled from underlying signalling procedures and may include multiple operations. The main characteristics of the two approaches are summarized in Table 1. Table 1 – Impacts on the different service approaches As an illustration example of the functional service class approach, a minimal set of service classes may be identified for the interactions across the RAN–CN boundary. These service classes are intended to capture broad functional capabilities rather than individual procedures. Similar grouping of capabilities can be observed in 5G CN [4], where services are organized around functional domains rather than individual procedures. Such functional classes may facilitate the identification of services and the definition of their associated roles, primitives, and data models. The following classes may be considered as an illustrative example of how functional capabilities exposed across the RAN–CN boundary could be grouped in a service-based interaction model: Context and State Exposure, enabling the exchange of context information and state-related data between RAN and CN entities. Control and Coordination, supporting control interactions and coordination actions between the involved entities. Analytics and Feedback, enabling the exchange of analytics information, measurements, and feedback that may support optimization or adaptation mechanisms. Lifecycle and Capability Management, supporting the management of capabilities, configuration aspects, and lifecycle-related interactions between the involved entities. Service roles The RAN–CN SBI uses service-dependent roles, consistent with the interaction model within the 5G CN [4]: a 6G RAN node (aNB) and a CN entity may act as producer, consumer, or both, depending on the service. The producer is the entity that exposes a service and provides the corresponding service operations, while the consumer is the entity that invokes the service. {"chunk_id":"R3-258444-002","collection":"ran3_tdoc_chunks","metadata":{"source":["CATT"],"tdocNumber":"R3-258444","title":"Discussion on general principles and requirements for 6G RAN"},"point_id":"521105928601913070"}
pics have received relatively high attention: Deployment flexibility: Proposals from Document R3-256571: The 6G RAN architecture shall allow flexible deployment that enables introduction of new 6G services in flexible manner during life cycle of 6G RAN with minimum or not impacting already deployed interface functions/services. Proposals from Document R3-256945: Base the 6G RAN design on the concept of modularity at function, protocol and interface procedure level, with the objective to support flexible distribution of 6G RAN processes. Proposals from Document R3-256904 and R3-256615: The 6G RAN architecture shall allow for deployment flexibility e.g. to host relevant RAN, CN and application functions close together at the edges of the network. Proposals from Document R3-256622: Migration from NR to 6GR will require procedure-level support for mobility, interoperability, and deployment flexibility across multiple scenarios. In addition, further migration options are expected to be studied in more detail during the 6G Radio SI. In 5G, the need to support diverse services such as low-latency communications means that deployment flexibility is an important requirement for architecture design, In 6G, with the emergence of various new services, such demands have become even more important for 6G architecture design. Therefore, it is proposed that, RAN3 could agree the following principles and requirements： - The 6G RAN architecture shall allow for deployment flexibility, e.g, in case a specific service or function is deployed for a particular objective, it will not affect or will minimally affect the existing interface function or services. 2）RAN Split architecture Proposals from Document R3-256571: The 6G RAN Architecture shall support both upper layer split and non-split RAN NF deployment scenarios. Proposals from Document R3-256615: The RAN architecture shall allow for CU-DU splitting. Proposals from Document R3-256687: 6GR architecture should continue support for dis-aggregated architecture. Proposals from Document R3-256622: The 6G RAN architecture should preserve the principle of functional separation established in NR, while reassessing the necessity of CP–UP split and confirming whether existing coordination mechanisms remain adequate for distributed deployments. Proposals from Document R3-256945: Handling of UE-associated functionalities such as UE configurations, UE state management, UE capability handling etc. shall be controlled by a single logical RAN entity. Proposals from Document R3-256539: This means the 6G RAN will be a single logical standardized entity comprising all RAN protocol stacks and functions. For detailed technical discussions on RAN split architecture, please refer to the topics in 10.3.2. However, as an important part of RAN architecture design, RAN3 needs to put forward corresponding principles and requirements. Similar to the relevant proposals in 5G, both split and non-split RAN deployment scenario should be supported in 6G, as the benefits of introducing the split architecture discussed in 5G remain valid. Nevertheless, considering that there are different viewpoints on this technical topic, the corresponding TP can be kept as FFS. Subsequently, the description can be revised again according to the final result of 10.3.2. Therefore, it is proposed that RAN3 could agree the following principles and requirements: - The RAN architecture shall allow both split and non-split RAN deployment scenarios. [FFS] 3）Independent Evolvement of RAN and CN Proposals from Document R3-256852: The 6G RAN architecture shall allow for the RAN and the CN to evolve independently. essing with radio functions. Disaggregation through a CU–DU split breaks this dependency and allows compute resources in the CU and DU domains to be scaled independently: CU capacity can be increased to address aggregate traffic and signaling demands across many cells, while DU resources can be scaled based on radio layer processing including channel bandwidth, total number of PRBs, number of MIMO layers, numerology, and the number of carriers handled by the DU, coverage and site-specific load. As a result, workload diversity across cells can be independently addressed. HLS architecture further allows functional decomposition of the CU into CU-CP and CU-UP entities [Section 6 of this document]. This separation allows the CU to be dimensioned according to finer workload granularity. Virtualization or cloudification of monolithic gNBs may improve infrastructure utilization. However, it does not solve the fundamental limitation: each gNB instance still handles its own control and user plane workloads, and peak provisioning must be dimensioned per instance. Workload variance across cells cannot be exploited, and CP/UP coupling remains, preventing independent scaling of signaling and throughput. Consequently, virtualization alone cannot achieve the resource efficiency and flexible scaling enabled by a CU-DU split. Observation : The HLS architecture achieves a three-dimensional scaling model, where CU-CP scales with UE count, CU-UP scales with user plane traffic demand, and DU scales with coverage. This is an advantage of disaggregated RAN architecture which is achievable independent of the deployment scenario. Proposal : We propose to delete the phrase “depending on the deployment scenarios” included in the benefit section of the TR, reflecting that resource pooling and elastic scaling are benefits achievable across all HLS-based deployment scenarios.

{"chunk_id":"R3-161900-002","collection":"ran3_tdoc_chunks","metadata":{"source":["Ericsson"],"tdocNumber":"R3-161900","title":"RAN Architecture and Specification Aspects"},"point_id":"15579045356772284818"}
alities. What is the granularity of the Centralized Unit – Distributed Unit functional split? As described in [1] the distribution of protocols and functions between a central and distributed unit may vary substantially depending on the deployment scenario. The standard should not focus on freezing the way functions can be distributed, but rather it should concentrate on designing functions in a modular way, so that they can be centralised or decentralized depending on the RAN deployment needs. Therefore the specifications should not determine a granularity for the function distribution but rather ensure a modular function design. With respect to which level of granularity a functional split should follow, it seems plausible to assume that functional splits can be supported on a per RAN BS. Multiple splits may be active within the same BS For the above the following answer is proposed: A3) The distribution of protocols and functions between a central and distributed unit may vary substantially depending on the deployment scenario. The standard should not focus on freezing the way functions can be distributed, but rather it should concentrate on designing functions in a modular way, so that they can be centralised or decentralized depending on the RAN deployment needs. Therefore the specifications should ensure a modular function design. With respect to which level of granularity it should be followed for a functional split, it is assumed that functional splits can be supported on a per RAN BS. Multiple splits may be active within the same BS What is the reconfiguration dynamicity of the network functional split? As discussed in [2] the distribution of functions between different logical units of the RAN should be configurable in order to meet deployment scenario requirements as they change. A re-distribution of functions within the RAN may occur when new services are introduced, when new sites are activated (and therefore there is the need for more coordination), when new user distributions are identified, when new transport networks are available, etc. These deployment conditions change in a way that is not too dynamic and therefore they can be met with new RAN architecture configurations. For the above the following answer is proposed: A4) The reconfiguration dynamicity of network functions splits depends on deployment scenario’s factors that are semi-persistent, such as offered services, site activation, users distribution, transport network availability. The reconfiguration of network functions distribution within the RAN can therefore be left to configuration. In this paper the discussion taken in [1] was used to formulate answers to the questions to be addressed in section 6.1.2.2 of TR38.801. It is proposed to agree to the TP below, which captures the answers presented.

In past meetings Low Layer Split architectures have been studied. Discussions have focussed on details relative to distribution of functions across a CU and DU entity, as well as what information could be exchanged over a possible interface between such entities. However, discussions so far have not tackled the full scope and applicability of the split architectures in question. This paper provides a first overview of areas where further analysis would be needed to evaluate the scope of this study.
